fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. Moses, Israel's leader, says it plain: “At the end of every seven years you must cancel debts.” Seven years go by, and the lender lets go of what his neighbor owes him. A creditor in that land had a standing appointment to let things go.

I understand the guess, because collecting is what a creditor normally does. But verse 2 turns that around: “He is not to collect anything from his neighbor or brother…” So when the seven years end, the lender doesn't collect. He cancels what he loaned, and the debt is gone, not just put on hold.

That's the reason in verse 2: “…because the LORD’s time of release has been proclaimed.” The lender doesn't stop because of a clever loophole or a bad mood. The release has been proclaimed, and it's the LORD's time of release. So the lender lets it go. That settles it.

Owing is a fair guess, because borrowing and owing go together like dough and an oven. But the blank wants the word that matches the first half of the promise. Verse 6 says, “you will lend to many nations but borrow from none…” The word the verse uses is lend, and owe never shows up.

Bowing sounds close, but it isn't the word in the verse. The text says Israel will “rule over many nations but be ruled by none.” The blank sits right where the verse says rule. Bow never appears in that verse.

Selling is a fair guess, since money talk shows up all over this passage. But verse 6 doesn't mention selling at all. It says Israel will lend to many nations but borrow from none, and rule over many nations but be ruled by none. Lend and rule are the words that fit the blanks.

That's it, baker. Verse 8 says, “Instead, you are to open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs.” The shut hand turns into an open hand. And the word is freely, so the Israelite is to loan whatever the man needs.

A tenth sounds like a tidy number, but verse 14 doesn't name a fraction. It says, “You shall give to him as the LORD your God has blessed you.” The master gives from his flock, his threshing floor and his winepress. The measure is his own blessing, not a set percentage.

That's the reason Moses gives. Verse 15 says, “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; that is why I am giving you this command today.” Israel knows from its own history what it was to be slaves and to be redeemed. Moses points them back to that when he gives the command about their servants.

Verse 15 doesn't mention the nations watching. It points Israel back to their own story. “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; that is why I am giving you this command today.” The reason lives in what Israel remembers, not in who might be looking.

That's right, baker. Verse 19 says, “You must set apart to the LORD your God every firstborn male produced by your herds and flocks.” Every one of them. The verse goes on to say the firstborn of the oxen aren't to be put to work, and the firstborn of the flock aren't to be sheared. Not a bad deal for an ox, while I'm over here stamping cookies all day.
